papers.title: Probable REM sleep behavior disorder and reduced cerebrospinal fluid 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid levels in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (RBD) in Parkinson's disease (PD) possibly involves dysfunction of the subcoeruleus and magnocellularis nuclei. Isolated RBD is associated with 123 METHODS: We retrospectively evaluated consecutive patients with PD who underwent CSF examinations between 2021 and 2025. pRBD was defined by the Japanese version of the RBD screening questionnaire score ≥6. Clinical characteristics, delayed MIBG heart-to-mediastinum (H/M) ratios, and CSF 5-HIAA levels were compared between patients with and without pRBD. Multivariable linear regression was performed using the log-transformed CSF 5-HIAA levels as the dependent variable. Mediation analyses evaluated whether MIBG H/M ratio mediated the association between pRBD and CSF 5-HIAA. RESULTS: Eighty-five patients were included (pRBD-negative, n = 70; pRBD-positive, n = 15). Patients with pRBD showed lower MIBG H/M ratios (p = 0.009) and CSF 5-HIAA levels (9.9 ± 3.3 vs. 14.5 ± 6.9 ng/mL, p < 0.001). pRBD positivity was associated with lower log-transformed CSF 5-HIAA after adjustment for age, sex, and disease duration (β = -0.33, p = 0.01). This association was attenuated after MIBG adjustment. Mediation analysis indicated that the MIBG H/M ratio statistically accounted for part of this association. CONCLUSION: pRBD in patients with PD was associated with reduced CSF 5-HIAA levels.

papers.title: Guam disease features chronic traumatic encephalopathy-like tau seeds in brain and spinal cord.
papers.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis/parkinsonism-dementia complex (ALS/PDC) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder that was once hyperendemic in the island of Guam (Mariana Islands, US) and a few other Pacific locales. Despite extensive investigations into its origins, the etiology of ALS/PDC remains unclear. ALS/PDC is, at the neuropathology level, characterized by tau-dominant multiple proteinopathy in brain and spinal cord. It was recently reported that Guam ALS/PDC brain extracts exhibit tau seeding activity in fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET)-based biosensor cells. To build upon those findings and explore the nature of tau seeds in ALS/PDC in more detail, we used an alanine mutational scanning (Ala scan) approach to determine the seeding profile of tau in nervous tissues of Guam ALS/PDC cases. First, we confirmed the detection of tau seeding activity in ALS/PDC brain samples in tau biosensor cells. Notably, we could also detect potent tau seeding activity in spinal cord. Subsequent Ala scan assays demonstrated that ALS/PDC tau displays an aggregate incorporation pattern that resembles that of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE)-type tau. This result is consistent with recent electron cryo-microscopy studies of tau, which revealed that ALS/PDC tau filaments are predominantly of the CTE-type. The structural characteristics and seeding behaviour of ALS/PDC tau, as well as the regional distribution of tau pathology at post-mortem, suggest that ALS/PDC is a CTE-like tauopathy.

papers.title: Comparative performance of nine large language models on professional Parkinson's disease tasks: a multidimensional benchmark study.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) requires both disease-specific knowledge and contextual clinical reasoning. However, most evaluations of medical large language models (LLMs) emphasize closed-ended questions and factual accuracy, providing limited insight into broader dimensions of performance on professional PD tasks. METHODS: Nine contemporary LLMs were evaluated using a 200-item English-language professional PD benchmark spanning five clinical domains, four difficulty levels, and multiple question formats. Responses were assessed for expert-rated factual accuracy, clinical reasoning, Global Quality Scale (GQS), and Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL). RESULTS: The nine models generated 1,800 responses. Between-model separation was minimal for expert-rated factual accuracy (Kendall' s W = 0.031) but greater for FKGL (W = 0.235), Clinical Reasoning (W = 0.256), and GQS (W = 0.301). Between-model separation in expert-rated factual accuracy was small for closed-ended questions (W = 0.020, p CONCLUSION: Contemporary LLMs showed limited between-model separation in expert-rated factual accuracy within this benchmark and scoring framework, whereas greater differentiation emerged in open-ended tasks, clinical reasoning, overall response quality, and readability. Multidimensional evaluation may therefore provide a more informative characterization of model performance and help inform task-specific model selection and oversight in medical applications.

papers.title: Neuroprotective actions of GLP-1 receptor agonists in Neurodegeneration: From mechanisms to clinical translation.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) have been explored as potential therapeutics for neurodegenerative disorders, yet a comprehensive integration of their neuroprotective mechanisms across Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and related conditions remains to be consolidated. This review examines the multimodal effects of GLP-1RAs on neuroinflammation, autophagy, mitochondrial function, and protein aggregation, with a focus on translational relevance and alignment between preclinical findings and clinical evidence. METHODOLOGY: A systematic synthesis of preclinical and clinical studies investigating GLP-1RA administration in neurodegenerative disease models and populations was conducted. Studies reporting neuroprotective outcomes and mechanistic pathways were included, and clinical trial data and real-world evidence for AD, PD, Huntington's disease, stroke, diabetic encephalopathy, and peripheral neuropathy were systematically evaluated. RESULTS: Preclinical evidence revealed that GLP-1RAs modulate key pathogenic processes, including amyloid-β and tau pathology, α-synuclein accumulation, neuroinflammatory cascades, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dynamics, endoplasmic reticulum stress, autophagy, and synaptic plasticity. Clinical data provided variable support, with emerging real-world evidence suggesting potential benefits. Novel strategies-such as dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists, enhanced blood-brain barrier penetration, and sustained-release formulations-were identified as promising approaches to improve efficacy, although significant gaps remain between preclinical promise and clinical outcomes. CONCLUSION: This review consolidates evidence that GLP-1RAs exert broad neuroprotective effects through multiple mechanisms, but clinical translation is still evolving. The potential of GLP-1-based therapies as disease-modifying interventions for neurodegeneration warrants further investigation, with particular att

papers.title: LLM-Guided Adaptive Cost Calibration in Active Learning for Parkinson's Disease Biosignals.
papers.abstract: Confirmatory labels for Parkinson's disease (PD), from expert examination or, prospectively, biological assays, are costly, and missed cases and false alarms carry unequal consequences. ClinRisk-LLM is a framework for label-efficient, cost-aware learning from gait and speech signals in which a large language model (LLM) translates a predefined safety specification into a frozen policy setting the positive-class weight of a support vector machine and the priority of potential missed cases for annotation. Cost-sensitive training, risk-aware querying and the LLM policy were ablated on gait (n=165) and speech (n=252) data and benchmarked against post hoc thresholding, a refer-all policy, held-out gait studies and an independent speech cohort. With half of the labels, cost-sensitive active learning reduced the 4:1 asymmetric cost by 34.1% (gait) and 5.7% (speech) relative to standard active learning, at the expense of specificity. ClinRisk-LLM translated the predefined safety specification into a frozen, auditable policy that adjusted risk settings during label acquisition. Component-wise analyses indicated that classifier weighting accounted for most of the observed cost reduction, while the incremental benefit of LLM-guided adaptation varied across datasets and comparison settings. A threshold-tuned symmetric model came within 1.3 cost points for gait, and gait remained roughly level with referring everyone. ClinRisk-LLM reached a gait cost of 47.60 versus 46.10 for fixed cost-sensitive learning; 40 policies generated across three LLMs from a reconstructed specification yielded gait costs of 52.1-75.8. Applications to molecular triage remain prospective. Code and data availability details are provided in the Data Availability Statement.

papers.title: Pantethine and Neurodegeneration: A Coenzyme A-Centered Framework Linking Metabolism, Neuroinflammation, and Mitochondrial Dysfunction.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are a growing global health burden associated with aging and characterized by progressive neuronal dysfunction, metabolic failure, mitochondrial impairment, oxidative stress, and chronic neuroinflammation. Among the metabolic pathways implicated in these disorders, coenzyme A (CoA)-linked biology has emerged as a potentially important but still underexplored contributor to neuronal resilience and vulnerability. Pantethine, a disulfide derivative of pantetheine and a CoA-related metabolic precursor, has attracted attention because of its reported effects on cellular metabolism, redox balance, and inflammatory signaling. However, its relevance across neurodegenerative diseases remains unevenly defined, with direct support strongest in pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN) and more limited evidence in common disorders such as Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD). This narrative review critically examines the mechanistic and translational evidence linking pantethine to neurodegeneration. PKAN represents the most logical disease context for pantethine investigation because impaired CoA biosynthesis is proximal to disease pathogenesis, although pantethine remains investigational and its clinical efficacy has not been established. By contrast, proposed applications in AD and PD remain highly theoretical and hypothesis-generating. Nevertheless, research on pantethine and related CoA-restoring strategies may identify new intervention targets across neurodegenerative diseases and other disorders characterized by impaired cellular bioenergetics, including selected neuropsychiatric disorders. These possibilities require biomarker-informed, disease-specific studies that establish active-species exposure, target engagement, and clinically meaningful effects.

papers.title: EEG-based Deep Learning Reveals Cortical Sensitivity to Small Changes in Deep Brain Stimulation Parameters.
papers.abstract: Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) is an invasive procedure used to alleviate motor symptoms in Parkinson's Disease (PD) patients. Despite its effectiveness, the impact of DBS on brain activity and the way to optimise stimulation parameters remains unclear. In this study, we aimed to map the sensitivity of cortical neural response to changes in DBS parameters in real-world clinical settings. We recorded in-clinic EEG data from PD patients during their clinical DBS programming sessions, both at rest and during arm movement. A siamese variant of the EEGNet deep learning architecture was trained independently for each patient and parameter combination to determine whether two 1-sec-long EEG segments were recorded under the same or different DBS parameters, yielding 30 independently trained models. Our models achieved an average accuracy of 74% in classifying whether two 1-second EEG segments corresponded to the same or different DBS parameters. Explainability methods were then applied to extract the neural oscillations learned by the models. Ablation studies identified mid-gamma oscillations (55-90Hz) as the key band for classifying these changes. Importantly, that was not driven by 1:2 gamma entrainment. In a sub-group of patients, the theta-alpha oscillations (4-12Hz) also contributed to detecting changes in DBS parameters. We demonstrate that small DBS parameter changes modify cortical activity in a consistent manner that can be detected using shallow convolutional networks on low-density EEG. Our findings suggest that cortical mid-gamma oscillations (55-90Hz) are highly sensitive to small changes in DBS settings. Our approach and findings could be leveraged towards identifying and defining novel digital biomarkers to guide DBS programming and adaptive DBS systems.

papers.title: 18F-FDG PET-revealed cognitive outcomes of subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease with cognitive impairment.
papers.journal: Neurotherapeutics : the journal of the American Society for Experimental NeuroTherapeutics

papers.title: The evolution of prion cell biology: from viruses to prions to prion-like proteins.
papers.abstract: Prion diseases are inevitably fatal, rare, and infectious neurodegenerative diseases of humans and animals. Initially, they were thought to be caused by unconventional slow viruses, and early research therefore relied heavily on experimental approaches used in virology. This view changed with the discovery that the causative agent of these diseases is not a virus but a conformational variant of a host-encoded protein. The conversion of the normally soluble host prion protein into an insoluble, infectious form enables the spread of pathology between cells and throughout the host. Over the past two decades, it has become clear that similar prion-like mechanisms of protein misfolding and templated self-propagation also underlie more common, non-infectious neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease. Thus, just as the cell biology of viruses provided important insights into the first studies of prion cell biology, discoveries in prion research have profoundly influenced our understanding of the cell biology of other amyloid-forming proteins. In this review, we discuss common principles and differences in the cell biology of prions and prion-like particles. We also highlight the seminal contributions of the late Dr. Byron Caughey and his laboratory, whose pioneering work has helped to shape our current understanding of how pathogenic protein aggregates form, propagate, and ultimately cause devastating neurological diseases.

papers.title: Transdiagnostic Mechanisms Underlying Nonaffective Psychosis: A Role for Hippocampal Networks?
papers.journal: The American journal of geriatric psychiatry : official journal of the American Association for Geriatric Psychiatry
papers.abstract: Psychosis is a functionally disruptive syndrome that results in an impaired sense of reality. People with psychosis have higher rates of mortality and institutionalization compared to the general population, necessitating evaluation and treatment in both neurologic and psychiatric practice. Effective treatments for psychosis require an understanding of the underlying neurobiological mechanisms that may be driving specific psychosis symptoms; however, previous efforts to assess these mechanisms have been challenging due to the heterogenous course and presentation. This review aims to provide a synthesis of what is currently known about psychosis and psychotic symptoms in primary and secondary nonaffective disorders, focusing on the most prevalent conditions in which these symptoms occur: schizophrenia, Parkinson's disease, and Alzheimer's disease. We review the phenomenology, prevalence, and natural history of psychosis in these disorders and highlight features and mechanisms thought to underlie specific psychosis symptoms across these disorders. The reviewed evidence reveals that psychosis is diagnosed differently depending on the disease context; however, the onset of well-formed psychotic symptoms is consistently preceded by a prodromal period in which attenuated symptoms present and insight is retained. In addition, symptoms are strongly linked to cognitive impairment, particularly short-term memory impairment, further supporting the notion of transdiagnostic mechanisms underlying psychosis. While this review provides an overview of key similarities and differences in psychosis symptoms across schizophrenia, Parkinson's disease, and Alzheimer's disease, more research is needed to explore several gaps identified in this review.

papers.title: Chronic Subdural Hematoma as a Potentially Reversible Cause of Cognitive and Gait Decline in Older Adults: Clinical Recognition, Treatment, and Functional Recovery.
papers.abstract: Chronic subdural hematoma (cSDH) is an increasingly common neurological disorder in older adults and may present with cognitive decline, gait instability, recurrent falls, and loss of independence rather than overt focal deficits. Because these symptoms overlap with dementia, delirium, parkinsonism, and frailty, diagnosis may be delayed despite the potential for meaningful recovery after treatment. This narrative review summarizes evidence on clinical recognition, treatment, early mobilization, rehabilitation, and patient-centered recovery in older adults with cSDH. A targeted search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science identified randomized trials, observational studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, guidelines, and consensus statements available through July 2026. Surgical decompression may improve cognition and mobility, but the magnitude and durability of recovery vary. Premorbid cognitive and functional status, frailty, malnutrition, postoperative delirium, and complications are associated with outcomes, although causal effects are incompletely established. Postoperative drainage reduces recurrence; selected randomized trials suggest that middle meningeal artery embolization reduces recurrence or treatment failure, whereas evidence for independent cognitive and gait benefits remains limited. Early mobilization may reduce medical complications. Evidence specific to cSDH remains insufficient to prescribe a standardized exercise dose or progression. Multidimensional follow-up and prospective trials using cognitive, gait, quality-of-life, and participation outcomes are needed to determine whether successful hematoma treatment translates into restored independence and meaningful daily function.

papers.title: Medial frontal infarction presenting with persistent unilateral gait initiation difficulty without paresis.
papers.abstract: A 79-year-old man developed sudden, persistent left-sided gait initiation difficulty and recurrent falls without weakness. Examination showed preserved strength, no parkinsonism, and an NIHSS score of 0. Brain MRI revealed a dominant right medial frontal infarct involving the ACA-MCA border-zone region, with more caudal extension into the expected distal ACA territory. This case highlights medial frontal infarction as a cause of asymmetric gait initiation difficulty despite preserved limb strength and minimal abnormalities captured by the NIHSS.

papers.title: MobileNetV2 for Multiclass Neurodegenerative Gait Analysis Using Bilateral Ground Reaction Force Images: From Transfer Learning to Raspberry Pi 4 Deployment.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs), including Parkinson's disease (PARK), Huntington's disease (HUNT), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), are associated with characteristic gait alterations. This study proposes an image-based deep-learning approach for NDD gait classification and its implementation on an edge-computing platform. The main contributions include: (1) mapping synchronized left- and right-foot ground reaction force (GRF) signals from individual gait cycles into a common 2D bilateral force space to generate three complementary representations-Trajectory Map (bilateral force trajectories), Derivative Map (dynamic transitions), and Occupancy Heatmap (loading-state distributions); (2) adapting ImageNet-pretrained MobileNetV2 to four-class gait classification (CONTROL, ALS, HUNT, and PARK) through classification-layer retraining and feature-extractor fine-tuning; (3) comparing compact (α = 0.35; ~0.4 M parameters) and higher-capacity (α = 1.4; ~4.4 M parameters) MobileNetV2 configurations; and (4) evaluating the deployment of the resulting models on a Raspberry Pi 4 as a resource-constrained edge-computing platform. The models were evaluated on a test subset of 2259 gait cycles from the Gait in Neurodegenerative Disease Database, comprising CONTROL (612), ALS (367), HUNT (727), and PARK (553). Fine-tuning increased overall four-class accuracy from 89.64-92.61% to 95.09-96.41% across the GRF representations and model configurations. Paired comparisons showed improvements of 3.81-6.29 percentage points across all six matched configurations. Class-specific one-vs-rest accuracy was consistently high after fine-tuning: CONTROL (97.74-98.63%), ALS (98.41-98.94%), HUNT (96.02-97.21%), and PARK (97.30-98.23%). The highest four-class accuracy (96.41%; 95% CI: 95.45-97.29%; Occupancy Heatmap, α = 1.4) was preserved for the unquantized TFLite model evaluated on the Raspberry Pi 4, while dynamic-range quantization reduced accuracy by 0.22 percentag

papers.title: Wavelet Scattering-Based Classification of Subthalamic Nucleus and Substantia Nigra Microelectrode Recordings During Deep Brain Stimulation Surgery.
papers.abstract: Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) surgery offers substantial improvements in quality of life for patients with Parkinson's disease. It consists of placing a stimulating electrode in the subthalamic nucleus (STN). Accurate and efficient localization of the target is essential because targeting errors may affect patient outcomes and the surgery is performed with the patient awake. Some systems already support neurosurgeons in the STN localization, but reliably separating the STN from the nearby substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) remains challenging. This study systematically evaluates the wavelet scattering transform for distinguishing STN from SNr under realistic DBS surgical constraints, where low-frequency information is unavailable and each recording must be classified independently in real time. Varying both the scattering parameters and the model complexity shows how these factors together influence performance. Classifiers ranging from support vector machines to temporal convolutional networks were capable of achieving balanced accuracy of 0.83-0.84 and receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC AUC) values of 0.91-0.93. This suggests that most discriminative information is captured by the wavelet scattering representation itself, resulting in robust performance across models of different complexity. The scattering-based approach achieved consistently higher performance than the evaluated wavelet packet-based baseline and highlights the potential of scattering-based representations for reliable STN localization during DBS surgery. However, the findings were obtained in a single-author, non-preregistered study using data acquired at a single center with a single recording system. Independent multicenter validation will therefore be necessary before broader clinical application can be considered.

papers.title: Human-Horse Neuromuscular Coordination Across Sequential Conditions During Physical Therapy Utilizing Equine Movement in Parkinson's Disease.
papers.journal: Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
papers.abstract: This exploratory, single-session, repeated-measures study characterized human and equine trunk muscle activity and human-horse EMG covariation during physical therapy utilizing equine movement in individuals with Parkinson's disease (PD). Nine individuals with PD and three horses completed pre-session quiet sitting (QS Pre), figure-eight riding (F8), stop-and-go riding (SNG), and post-session quiet sitting (QS Post). Bilateral surface EMG was recorded from three human and four equine trunk muscles. All analyses were exploratory and examined four outcomes: normalized EMG amplitude, zero-lag human-horse correlation, lagged human-horse correlation, and human-horse EMG-EMG coherence. Human normalized EMG amplitude did not differ across QS Pre, F8, and SNG. Equine amplitude was greater during F8 than QS Pre (difference 9.43 percentage points, 95% CI [4.27, 14.59]). SNG also showed greater amplitude than QS Pre (5.30 percentage points, 95% CI [0.32, 10.27]), although this difference was not statistically significant in the participant-level sensitivity analysis. F8 exceeded SNG in the direct comparison (4.43 percentage points, 95% CI [1.44, 7.41]) but not in the adjusted three-condition comparison. Zero-lag correlations were generally close to zero; SNG exceeded F8 by only 0.0056 Fisher's z units (95% CI [0.0004, 0.0107]) in the direct comparison, but this difference was not statistically significant in the adjusted three-condition comparison. When temporal offsets of ±300 ms were permitted, lagged correlation strength was greater during F8 than QS Pre (difference 0.013, 95% CI [0.003, 0.024]) and during SNG than QS Pre (0.011, 95% CI [0.001, 0.021]), with no difference between riding conditions. Median wavelet coherence was greater during QS Pre than F8 (difference 0.016, 95% CI [0.013, 0.018]) or SNG (0.013, 95% CI [0.011, 0.015]), while SNG exceeded F8 overall (0.003, 95% CI [0.002, 0.004]). papers.title: TNF rs1800629 Genotype and Motor Response to Intensive Rehabilitation in Parkinson's Disease: An Exploratory Study.
papers.abstract: Rehabilitation is a key component of Parkinson's disease (PD) management, although individual responses differ substantially. Genetic factors involved in neuroplasticity and inflammation may contribute to this variability. We investigated whether selected polymorphisms in inflammation- and neuroplasticity-related genes influence motor outcomes following intensive multidisciplinary rehabilitation in patients with PD. papers.title: Temporal evolution of EEG band power at freezing of gait onset in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Although EEG studies have implicated theta-, alpha-, and beta-band activity in freezing of gait (FoG) in Parkinson's disease (PD), most have relied on resting-state comparisons, task contrasts, or connectivity analyses rather than modeling band-power changes around FoG onset. This study investigated the temporal evolution of EEG spectral power around FoG onset during ecological walking. METHODS: We analyzed a multimodal dataset comprising 10 individuals with PD and FoG during ecological walking. Two hundred and four FoG episodes were analyzed. EEG was recorded from 25 scalp electrodes and time-locked to FoG onset. Relative spectral power was computed for theta, alpha, and beta bands. Channel-wise piecewise linear mixed-effects models evaluated pre-FoG trends, onset-related shifts, and post-onset slope changes. Multiple comparisons were controlled using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR, q < 0.05). RESULTS: Theta power showed no significant pre-FoG trend but increased abruptly at FoG onset at F3 and Fz. Alpha power exhibited a progressive pre-FoG increase at FP1, F3, F8, Fz, and Cz, whereas no onset-related or post-onset alpha effects survived FDR correction. Beta power showed no significant temporal modulation after correction. These findings indicate temporal profiles, with alpha changes preceding FoG and theta changes emerging at onset. CONCLUSION: FoG onset during ecological walking is associated with dissociable low-frequency EEG dynamics. Frontal and midline alpha increases may characterize a pre-freezing state, whereas abrupt frontal theta increases are associated with the transition into FoG. These patterns represent candidate electrophysiological features that require prospective validation before predictive or biomarker applications can be established.

papers.title: The Circadian Diet in Age-Related Neurodegeneration: Nutrient Timing, Sleep, and Mitochondrial Mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms coordinate sleep-wake regulation, endocrine secretion, nutrient handling and cellular energy metabolism. Circadian and sleep disturbances are associated with metabolic and cardiovascular morbidity and with neurodegenerative disorders, particularly Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD), although whether restoring circadian alignment modifies neurodegeneration remains uncertain. This narrative review examines chrononutrition within the broader context of sleep regulation, physical activity and circadian care, distinguishing evidence from cellular and animal models, observational studies and clinical trials. papers.title: Ergothioneine: A Natural Antioxidant Claimed to Prevent Neurodegeneration.
papers.abstract: Ergothioneine (ET) is an exogenous thiol antioxidant present mainly in mushrooms and, in smaller amounts, in various other food products as well. Numerous beneficial health effects of ET have been reported, suggesting that ET is a vitamin-like compound. Evidence that ET prevents and inhibits the development of neurodegenerative diseases, especially Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease, has been accumulated based on studies of cellular and animal models, as well as epidemiologic and interventional studies in humans. The mechanism of the neuroprotective action of ET remains to be elucidated. Apart from the direct antioxidant effect, ET was found to stimulate an endogenous antioxidant defense through the activation of Nrf2 signaling while also affecting other signaling pathways. The accumulating literature data suggest that an ET-rich diet could be recommended for the prevention of neurodegeneration in the general population, but such a recommendation, though noteworthy, is not yet adequately supported by the limited human intervention data, and further studies are needed.

papers.title: Outpatient Supportive and Palliative Care for Parkinson's Disease and Related Disorders: A Scoping Review.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease and related disorders (PDRD) are chronic neurodegenerative diseases which cause significant disability related to a range of motor, non-motor, and neurobehavioral symptoms. The heterogeneous and progressive symptom burden often necessitates substantial time and ongoing support from those who help to coordinate and provide care; this is true both in formal health care settings and of informal caretakers within the patient's personal life. Significant physical and emotional burden therefore not only directly impacts patients but also extends to their support systems. Palliative and supportive care have well-established benefits in other high symptom burden fields, such as oncology. Though their applications in PDRD are newer and less established, a number of palliative and supportive care interventions for this population have been developed and monitored in recent years. In order to consolidate and appraise the evidence supporting palliative and supportive care for PDRD, we performed a scoping review synthesizing the literature published between 2009 and 2026 that explored how these programs have been implemented and what their effects have been on (a) patient quality of life, (b) motor symptoms, (c) non-motor symptoms, (d) advance care planning, and (e) care partner quality of life and/or burden. We identified 10 relevant studies, which collectively demonstrate benefits in each of the aforementioned domains for patients and care partners participating in the palliative/supportive care intervention, though with some variation in impact possibly related to differences in care delivery model, setting, and study design. We also acknowledge the huge range of mechanisms by which palliative or supportive care principles may be applied to PDRD and briefly discuss additional approaches not captured by our formal review. Overall, this summary aims to inform the development and refinement of evidence-based palliative and supportive care models for individua

papers.title: Research highlights and trends in the field of swallowing disorders in Parkinson's disease over the past decade: A bibliometric analysis.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: The study aimed to analyze research hotspots and trends in swallowing dysfunction in Parkinson's disease over the past decade (2015-2025). METHODS: Articles published from 2015 to 2025 were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection on March 14, 2026, and 813 articles were included. CiteSpace 6.4.R1 and VOSviewer were used to map countries, institutions, authors, journals, references, and keywords. Annual output was tested with linear regression and the Mann-Kendall test, and research impact was assessed with citation-based indicators, including the h-index, citations per publication, and year-normalized citation scores. RESULTS: Annual output increased from 40 articles in 2015 to 113 in 2025 (6.2 additional articles per year; R2 = 0.78, P < .001). The 813 articles received 12,064 citations (h-index = 48). The United States accounted for the highest number of publications, with the majority of authors concentrated in Europe and the United States. Internationally coauthored articles had higher year-normalized citation scores than single-country articles (1.54 vs 0.85, P = .002). Keyword co-occurrence analysis revealed that the research focus is gradually shifting from interventions targeting individual symptoms toward holistic patient management, with an emphasis on patient-centered care and improving quality of life. CONCLUSION: Research on dysphagia in Parkinson's disease has grown steadily and has moved from mechanism and instrumental assessment studies toward prognosis, medication-related swallowing problems, and quality of life. These bibliometric patterns describe research attention and do not establish clinical effectiveness. They point to evidence gaps in standardized screening, early detection, intervention trials, and digital assessment that warrant further clinical studies and wider international collaboration.

papers.title: A New Selection Strategy to Enrich Dopaminergic Neurons Facilitates Comparisons Between Patient iPSC-Derived Lines.
papers.abstract: Comparative studies of dopaminergic (DA) neurons differentiated from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) derived from patients discordant for parkinsonism, especially siblings, provide a valuable model to explore factors underlying Parkinson disease (PD) pathogenesis. However, such studies are complicated by the inherent heterogeneity in differentiation efficiency among iPSC lines derived from different individuals. To address this technical challenge, we devised a selection strategy to enrich DA neurons expressing tyrosine hydroxylase (TH). A neomycin resistance gene (neo
